name: Walking speed - working-age adult
applies_to: age_years >= 18 and age_years < 65 and mobility != wheelchair
finding: Comfortable adult walking speed about 1.20 m/s with sd near 0.24 m/s.
notes: The spread matters as much as the mean: it is what makes a crowd have a slow tail.

name: Walking speed - 65 and over
finding: Older adults are markedly slower than able-bodied adults on the level and on stairs.
notes: The mean is reasoned from the simulation's sourced elderly range rather than read off a table. Needs the Fire Technology 2024 trial pinned down.

name: Walking speed - under 18
finding: Children are slower than adults; small children occupied the full stair width and were not carried.
notes: Proulx measured 0.33 m/s on stairs for 2-5 year olds, which is a stair figure, not this level figure.

name: Walking speed - wheelchair
finding: Assisted and wheeled occupants are much slower than able-bodied adults.
notes: Range reasoned from the simulation's sourced wheelchair profile. These occupants cannot use stairs at all, which matters far more than their level speed.

name: Walking speed - ambulatory difficulty
finding: Occupants who walk with difficulty move at about two thirds of the able-bodied speed.
notes: Applied on top of the age-based speed, so an older person with a cane gets both effects.

name: Carrying or handling a pet
finding: A pet occupies a hand and slows both level and stair movement by about a tenth.
notes: Carried over as a claim from the team's first workbook (rule S103). No source was attached to it there and none has been found since.

name: Patience behind a blockage
finding: How long somebody stands in a stalled queue before giving up on that staircase.
notes: The simulation uses 40-80 s and flags it as invented. Queue tolerance measured in lift queues runs 1-5 minutes, so this is probably too impatient. Worth an early sensitivity run.

name: Tries the other staircase after turning back
finding: Of those who turn back from smoke, about a quarter try the other staircase rather than going home.
notes: Matches the simulation's sourced other_stair_share. The source behind that value still needs recording here.

name: Milling - baseline
finding: About 70 percent of WTC occupants milled - sought information or conferred - before evacuating.
notes: NIST's figure is for an office population. A residential tower at night may differ, and that difference is one of the things this project is for.

name: Milling - a new tenant has fewer people to confer with
finding: Milling is information-seeking from other people; somebody who knows nobody in the building has fewer to seek it from.
notes: Reasoned, not measured. Proulx supports that residents rely on familiar people and routes, not this size of effect.

name: Milling - living alone
finding: Conferring with a household member is the commonest first response; somebody alone skips it.
notes: Reasoned from Proulx's finding that 62 percent left in groups.

name: Seeks a second cue before moving
finding: Looking for confirmation - the hallway, a neighbour, a siren, the news - before accepting that an alarm is real.
notes: NIST lists looking for confirmation as a behaviour pattern but gives no per-person propensity, so the distribution is ours.

name: Seeks a second cue - poor alarm
finding: A corridor-only alarm is ambiguous where an in-flat alarm is not.
notes: The alarm effect on time to start is well measured; routing it through this disposition rather than straight into a delay is our modelling choice.

name: Compliance with instructions
finding: Willingness to act on an alarm or an announcement rather than reinterpret it.
notes: In the real residential cases nearly every later instruction came from firefighters in person, which this does not yet capture.

name: Altruism
finding: 30 to 34 percent of WTC occupants helped others; 23 to 32 percent searched for others.
notes: An office population with no family present still spent this much effort on others, so a residential figure is likely higher.

name: Leadership
finding: Tendency to direct others rather than follow.
notes: No measurement found. Named as a factor in the project's reading but never quantified.

name: Leadership - head of household
finding: One member typically decides for the household and the rest follow.
notes: Reasoned from households deciding together.

name: Risk tolerance
finding: Willingness to enter a route they can see is degraded.
notes: Drives the smoke turn-back decision, which the simulation currently draws from a population share rather than a disposition.

name: Risk tolerance - 65 and over
finding: Older occupants were more likely to shelter than to attempt a degraded route.
notes: A guess consistent with the Forest Laneway pattern, where most early evacuation attempts failed and residents sheltered.

name: Knows the building - new tenant
finding: Residents chose familiar stairs over the nearest ones.
notes: Proulx supports the mechanism; the three tenure bands and their means are ours.

name: Knows the building - one to five years
finding: As above.

name: Knows the building - five years or more
finding: As above.

name: Knows a second staircase exists - new tenant
finding: Whether they know there is another way down at all.
notes: Nobody has measured this and it may matter a great deal, because not knowing removes the alternative the model relies on.

name: Knows a second staircase exists - established resident
finding: As above.

name: Habitual staircase
finding: Residents chose familiar stairs over the nearest, so each has a habit to reach for.
notes: Split evenly for want of anything better. In a real building the split follows which stair is nearer each flat.

name: False alarms lived through - one to five years
finding: How many times the bell has already cried wolf here.
notes: Both effects are documented for the 1993 WTC bombing - experience made some faster and some slower - and nothing here yet uses this field.

name: False alarms lived through - five years or more
finding: As above.

name: Fire safety training
finding: Any drill or training in this building.
notes: Residential towers rarely drill; a tenth is a guess.

name: Hears the alarm - good alarm
finding: In the buildings with an alarm inside each flat every occupant heard it.
notes: Audibility was the single largest driver of time to start: 169 s audible against 515 s poor.

name: Hears the alarm - poor alarm
finding: Between 23 and 25 percent of residents did not hear a corridor-only alarm from inside the flat; 24 percent at Forest Laneway.

name: Pre-movement time
finding: Good-alarm residential cluster: Weibull scale 102.475 s, shape 0.767, n = 149. Implied mean 120 s.
notes: PARKED ON PURPOSE, and switched off. The simulation already fits this from the same source, per scenario and by time of day, and the two clusters differ by a factor of six. Setting it here would freeze one cluster into every run. Left in the registry because the value is the right one to argue about, and because it records why we do not emit it.
